nameStory: This rare sedge carries the name of botanist Douglass Houghton, Michigan's first state geologist who explored the Great Lakes region in the 1830s. The 'umbrella' part comes from the way its flower clusters are arranged at the top of the stem, radiating outward like the spokes of an umbrella.
description: Houghton's Umbrella-sedge is one of New England's rarest plants, a small grass-like sedge that grows in clumps. This delicate plant typically reaches 6-18 inches tall with narrow, green leaves and small brownish flower clusters arranged in an umbrella-like pattern at the stem tips. It's part of the sedge family, which are grass-like plants but have triangular stems instead of round ones.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Feel the stem between your fingers - it's distinctly triangular in cross-section, not round like a grass. The old saying goes 'sedges have edges' to help remember this key difference.

idTips.label: Flower Clusters
idTips.description: Small brownish clusters arranged like umbrella spokes at the stem top, typically 3-8 clusters radiating outward from the same point. Each cluster contains tiny scale-like flowers.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, grass-like leaves that feel smooth to the touch and are usually shorter than the flowering stems. They grow mainly from the base of the plant.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small tufts or loose colonies, never covering large areas. Individual plants look delicate and wispy compared to robust wetland sedges.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Stays relatively small at 6-18 inches tall, making it easy to overlook among taller wetland plants. The entire plant has a fine, delicate texture.

habitat: Look for Houghton's Umbrella-sedge in sandy or gravelly shores of lakes and ponds, particularly where the water level fluctuates seasonally. It prefers open, sunny spots with mineral-rich soils rather than peaty wetlands. In New England, it's most likely found along the shores of larger lakes and occasionally in wet sandy areas near the coast.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge from the ground, and the triangular stems become apparent. Early leaf growth begins as the plant prepares for its summer flowering period.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs from mid to late summer, when the characteristic umbrella-shaped flower clusters appear. This is the best time for identification when the diagnostic features are most visible.
seasonality.fall: Flowers mature into small brown seed heads that may persist into early fall. Leaves begin to yellow and the plant prepares to die back for winter.
seasonality.winter: The above-ground parts die back completely, leaving only the root system alive underground. No visible plant parts remain for identification during the cold months.

funFact: With only 7 recorded observations in all of New England, you're more likely to spot a rare bird than this elusive sedge - it's so uncommon that finding one would be a genuine botanical treasure hunt success!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small flatsedges, especially Umbrella Flatsedge which has a similar flower arrangement. The key difference is size and habitat - Houghton's is generally smaller and prefers sandy lake shores, while Umbrella Flatsedge is more common in muddy areas and wet fields.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'sedge,' this plant belongs to the flatsedge group within the sedge family, which typically have umbrella-like flower arrangements rather than the spike-like flowers of true sedges. The extreme rarity in New England makes any sighting worth documenting and reporting to local botanists.
compareHints: Among its flatsedge relatives, Houghton's Umbrella-sedge is distinguished by its small size and preference for sandy lake shores rather than muddy wetlands. While Yellow Nutsedge and Straw-colored Flatsedge are much more common and robust, Houghton's maintains a delicate, wispy appearance and stays close to fluctuating water levels of natural lakes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many flatsedge species, straw-colored flatsedge stands out for its relatively tall height and branching, airy flower clusters.

Among New England's flatsedges, yellow nutsedge is distinctive for its bright golden-yellow flowers and robust growth habit - most other flatsedges have brownish or straw-colored flowers and are generally smaller.
Among New England's flatsedges, toothed flatsedge is unique in reliably producing bulblets, which sets it apart from relatives like yellow nutsedge or straw-colored flatsedge.
Among its flatsedge relatives, shining flatsedge stands out for its particularly glossy flower scales - most other Cyperus species have duller, more matte-colored scales.

Among New England's many flatsedges, Great Plains flatsedge is distinguished by its compact, clumping growth habit and relatively small size compared to the taller, more sprawling straw-colored flatsedge.
Among New England's flatsedges, bearded flatsedge is distinguished by its prominently bristly flower clusters that truly look bearded.
Among its many flatsedge cousins in New England, redroot flatsedge stands alone with those brilliant red roots - no other Cyperus species has this feature.

Among New England's flatsedges, Engelmann's is distinguished by its relatively small size and compact flower clusters compared to the much taller straw-colored flatsedge or the more robust yellow nutsedge.
Among New England's flatsedges, umbrella flatsedge stays notably short and compact compared to the much taller straw-colored flatsedge or yellow nutsedge.
Among its flatsedge relatives, small-flower halfchaff sedge is distinguished by its particularly tiny flower clusters and more delicate build.
Among New England's flatsedges, Gray's is distinguished by its relatively large size and the specific arrangement of its flower clusters.
Asian flatsedge is smaller and more delicate than most of its flatsedge relatives like straw-colored flatsedge or yellow nutsedge.
Among New England's many flatsedges, fern flatsedge stands out for its particularly delicate, finely-branched flower clusters that are more lacy and open than most relatives.
Among New England's flatsedges, fragrant flatsedge is distinguished by its sweet scent when crushed and its preference for consistently moist soils.

Among New England's flatsedges, variable flatsedge is distinguished by its very compact, ball-like flower clusters rather than the loose, umbrella-shaped arrangements of umbrella flatsedge or the elongated spikes of yellow nutsedge.
Among New England's flatsedges, brown flatsedge is distinguished by its rich chocolate-brown flower clusters - most other flatsedges have yellow, straw-colored, or greenish flowers.
Rice flat-sedge is smaller and more delicate than most of its flatsedge relatives in New England, such as the much taller straw-colored flatsedge or the robust yellow nutsedge.
Yellow flatsedge is much smaller and more delicate than its relatives like yellow nutsedge, which has underground tubers, or straw-colored flatsedge, which grows much taller.
Among its flatsedge relatives, Asiatic greenhead sedge is notably smaller and more compact than yellow nutsedge or straw-colored flatsedge.
Among New England's flatsedges, Globe Flatsedge stands out for its perfectly round, compact flower clusters - most others like Yellow Nutsedge have more open, branched arrangements.
Japanese flatsedge is generally smaller and more compact than the common yellow flatsedge, and lacks the distinctive straw-colored appearance of straw-colored flatsedge.
Pinebarren flatsedge is shorter and has cylindrical flower clusters compared to most of its flatsedge relatives.
